pos.personaBrief: Inter's catenaccio gave up the ball and countered (Sacchi, SI transitions, Picchi sitting back, Suarez long balls); Mazzola says more attacking football, but the core was counter-attack with few touches.

pro.personaBrief: Herrera's own quote: few very quick passes to reach goal in little time, almost no dribbling; Suarez hit long balls from deep.

est.personaBrief: Rigid roles under man-marking, libero and set assignments (Picchi sweeper, Facchetti the left flank, Jair the right), strict drilled structure.

lar.personaBrief: Attacks came through Facchetti and Jair on the flanks and counters with attacking full-backs, plus Corso on the left; the central creator Suarez played deep.

blo.personaBrief: Inter went ahead then sat back, four man-markers plus libero, 5-3-2 (SI, Forza); conceded 20 goals in 34 games in 1963; no pressing evidence.

mar.personaBrief: Man-to-man marking by four defenders with a free libero, verified in several sources; he would favour clear individual responsibility.

pla.personaBrief: Imposed his model and discipline on every club (Angelillo thrown out, Picchi shipped out), kept files on opponents and set up cautious catenaccio against strong sides.

res.personaBrief: Turned to catenaccio in desperation to win; 'we only need one goal'; 'I don't know failure'; result above all.

sis.personaBrief: Obedience over individualism: no individual quality trumped obedience; stars like Corso, Angelillo and Picchi were disciplined; the drilled system came first.

jog.personaBrief: Brutal ritiro training camps, demanding pace work, 'passion and strength', Jair hard-running, but also technicians like Suarez.

bas.personaBrief: Built title teams with signed established players (Suarez, Picchi, Jair, Hitchens); no academy emphasis.

lid.personaBrief: Strict disciplinarian: ritiro, curfew checks, suspensions for loose words, stars removed; though he used psychology and confessions, he was the boss.
